flawed_step: To prove the statement, you would need to show that some choice of two edges at every vertex can always be extended to a Hamiltonian cycle. This cannot be justified. Tutte fragments are 3-connected cubic planar pieces that force every Hamiltonian cycle to use one specific attaching edge. Attaching three fragments to one vertex by those forced edges makes a Hamiltonian cycle impossible.
counterexample: The Tutte graph (Tutte, 1946). Take a central vertex v and three copies F1, F2, F3 of the Tutte fragment. Each fragment has 15 vertices and three outgoing edges a, b, c, and all its vertices have degree 3 once those edges are counted. Its defining property: any Hamiltonian cycle of the whole graph enters and leaves the fragment through two of these edges, one of which must be a; the pair {b,c} is impossible. Join v to the a-edge of each Fi. Join b(F1) to c(F2), b(F2) to c(F3), and b(F3) to c(F1). The result has 46 vertices and 69 edges. It is cubic, planar (fragments placed around v), and 3-connected. A Hamiltonian cycle would have to use a(F1), a(F2) and a(F3). All three meet at v, but a cycle uses only 2 edges at any vertex. So no Hamiltonian cycle exists.
assessment_summary: The statement is Tait's conjecture, which is false. The Tutte graph (46 vertices) is a 3-connected cubic planar graph with no Hamiltonian cycle, because three fragments each force the cycle to use their edge to the same central vertex. The fragment's internal edge list was described from memory, not written out in full; the graph's properties are the classical, well-established result.
